topPRs.title: op-core,kona: model super-root dispute game and EthLockbox addresses
topPRs.author: pauldowman
topPRs.body:
The superchain-registry `Addresses` struct is mirrored by `op-core/superchain`'s `AddressesConfig` and kona's `AddressList`. Both had drifted from it: `EthLockboxProxy` was never added, and superchain-registry#1353 adds `SuperFaultDisputeGame` and `SuperPermissionedDisputeGame` for chains that have moved to Upgrade 20 super-root games.

`op-core/superchain` decodes registry chain configs with `DecodeTOMLStrict` and no allowed-unknown keys, so a key the struct does not model is a hard load failure; kona silently drops one instead. Keeping the mirrors complete is the invariant `op-core/superchain/chain.go` documents.

- `AddressesConfig` and `AddressList` gain `SuperFaultDisputeGame`, `SuperPermissionedDisputeGame` and `EthLockboxProxy`.
- The two super-root game impls join `AddressList::zero_proof_addresses`; `EthLockboxProxy` does not, since it is a core rather than a fault-proof contract.
- `rust/kona/crates/protocol/registry/etc/configs.json` is regenerated, as `kona-registry-snapshot-check` requires. `AddressList` serializes `None`, so this is 3 null lines per chain across 53 chains and no other change.

Scope: this is schema only. Both mirrors read the per-chain TOML `[addresses]` tables, which carry only the essential addresses, so the new fields stay null until the registry publishes them there. No consumer gains data today.

Follow-up, not done here: `AddressList` is the only nested kona chain-config struct without `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` — `roles.rs`, `altda.rs`, `hardfork.rs` and `ChainConfig` all have it. That asymmetry is why kona drops an unmodeled registry key silently where Go fails loudly, and it is the reason this kind of drift goes unnoticed on the Rust side.
